label: Constitutively simple: at most one real constituent, non-real items not counted
term: constitutively simple (ConstitutivelySimple RealConstituent g); real constituent (RealConstituent g a)
definition: ConstitutivelySimple RealConstituent g: any two real constituents of g are identical, so g has at most one real constituent. RealConstituent g a: a is a real constituent of g, something in g that has being in reality as a part, principle, property or aspect of g, independently of being an object of any apprehension or a term of any relation of reason. Examples of real constituents: the matter and form of a body; the several real powers of a composite agent; the several real representations (concepts, mental states) of a human thinker; the one nature of a simple source. Non-examples: an object of understanding as understood (on the classical account, a divine idea, which is the one essence as understood under a respect); a negation or privation considered as an item; a mode of imitability on the rival account that holds it is in the nature without being a real constituent. Structural properties: RealConstituent is a declared primitive two-place relation; constitutive simplicity is the statement that the set of real constituents of g is a subsingleton (Mathlib Set.Subsingleton is the generic counterpart). It counts real constituents only and therefore does not by itself deny a plurality of descriptions, intentional relata or other non-real items in g.
